review.title: A real catalog metadata source
review.notes: The discovery layer has no metadata source. PL-0105 landed a seam, and docs/CATALOG_SOURCE.md says so in its first line; this task is the thing that belongs behind it, tracked so the gap stays visible instead of being hidden by a port that looks finished. docs/PRODUCT_SPEC.md step 2 of the initial user journey is browse/search normalized metadata, and nothing in this repository ingests any: every surface reads six fictional works. PL-0301 and PL-0302 do not close it - they supply stream candidates, which is what a title plays from, not what a catalog is made of. PARTLY BLOCKED, and the split is deliberate rather than a hedge. The design half - identity and dedupe, refresh and staleness, tombstones, paging, provider-side search, the locale-tagged contract, and the undeclared-rights state that catalogItemSchema cannot currently express - needs no external access and can begin now. Connecting an actual metadata provider, and carrying artwork, cannot: both need an agreement and credentials, which control/policies.json escalates to human-only under Licensing and Credentials - the same categories that block PL-0302. It is a DIFFERENT agreement from PL-0302's, covering catalog metadata and image rights rather than stream rights, so this is not merely waiting on that task; the honest status is BACKLOG with the ceiling named, not BLOCKED on someone else's licence.
review.acceptance: A metadata source stands behind resolveCatalogMetadataSource and answers what the port deliberately does not. Ingestion: something fetches, schedules and backfills, rather than an array being maintained by hand. Refresh: an answer carries its age and a stated staleness policy, so nobody has to guess how old a rail is. Identity and dedupe: how a provider's native id becomes a normalizedContentId, and what happens when two sources describe the same work, is settled as a design decision before it is coded - this is the largest missing piece and it is not a coding question. Deletion: a work that disappears from a source produces a tombstone, so it stays distinguishable from a fetch that failed. Paging and provider-side search: listRecords returning everything is a shape only six fixtures can use, and who owns ranking and paging is part of the contract rather than an accident of in-memory filtering. Artwork: images arrive with their own licensing, tracked separately from the work's, or they do not arrive. Localization and availability: title, genre and synopsis are locale-tagged and a work can be offered in more than one language, and availability windows and territory exist, so the empty state's claim about a region is backed by something. Every record declares a rights basis whose category agrees with its item and whose reference is an opaque internal identifier or null, and the ingestion path is treated as untrusted third-party I/O - allowlisted egress, bounded bodies, redirects revalidated, and no media address anywhere in a catalog payload.

THE COMMANDER'S LICENSING DECISION IS NOW IMPLEMENTED: Wikidata stands behind resolveCatalogMetadataProvider, which closes the first acceptance clause that round 44 correctly refused to claim. The port did not move -- wikidata.ts imports FROM provider.ts and nothing in the port imports back, and ingest, project, identity, freshness and safety never mention Wikidata -- which is what keeps the decision an INITIAL source choice rather than a shape baked into the seam. CAPABILITIES ARE DECLARED HONESTLY RATHER THAN OPTIMISTICALLY, each measured: providerSideSearch true; incrementalSince FALSE because WDQS's default graph binds nothing for schema:version or dateModified and the Action API that has them costs a measured 206 KB per entity, so changedSince is ignored entirely rather than silently approximated; reportsDeletions FALSE because deletions need a different API; maxPageSize 50, the number the source itself uses; and sourceRevision ALWAYS NULL, which is a real gap stated as one -- a consumer cannot tell whether a record changed between passes. Enumeration is keyset-paged on the numeric QID rather than OFFSET, because CirrusSearch hard-fails at offset 10,000, measured. THE CC0 / CC BY-SA DISTINCTION IS ENFORCED BY FOUR MECHANICAL CONTROLS, NOT DOCUMENTED: a frozen two-host set with construction refused if the operator's egress allowlist names anything else, so en.wikipedia.org in the policy yields NO provider; an entity-id pattern admitting only Q, P and L, with Commons M-ids refused by name; no SERVICE clause in any built query, asserted; and no request for P18, P154, P3383, sitelinks or extracts, with artwork always empty and unable to be otherwise. THE USER-AGENT OBLIGATION IS STRUCTURAL: the option stays required with no default, createWikidataProvider additionally refuses an agent string with no contact token or with a browser token by two separate named refusals, and a ts-expect-error test fails if a default is ever added -- a bad agent gets no provider rather than an IP block. RIGHTS MACHINERY ON REAL RECORDS: the rights register is required with no default and noRightsBasisEstablished must be passed BY NAME, so a default composition against real Wikidata publishes NOTHING, asserted over three recorded real films -- that is the correct outcome, not a bug. P6216 is read and not interpreted. The pre-parse media-address scan now has an untrusted writer behind it, since a Wikidata label is editable by anyone logged in and a vandalised title reading like a manifest URL is an ordinary string to the schema; the test is built from a real response with one label replaced. A FINDING THE IMPLEMENTER GOT BY WRITING THE TEST AND GETTING THE OTHER ANSWER: a rights reference carrying a contract URL is refused as media_address_in_catalog_payload rather than as a non-opaque reference, because the address scan runs first. ROUND 44'S TRIPWIRE FIRED AND WAS INVERTED RATHER THAN DELETED: the licensed-source set is frozen, holds only wikidata, throws on runtime mutation and licenses no keyed source, and a tmdb request is refused by name. LIVE TESTS ARE OUT OF THE GATE: wikidata.live.test.ts hits the real service, is excluded by the package vitest config, reachable only through a separate script, and was run deliberately -- 3 passed in 20.4s -- but is not what this gate rests on.

licensingDecision.decision: Wikidata is the initial catalog metadata source.
licensingDecision.rationale: It requires no credential and keeps the provider seam replaceable.
licensingDecision.scope: INITIAL SOURCE CHOICE, NOT AN EXCLUSIVE OR PERMANENT SOURCE MANDATE. Recorded in those words at the reviewer's insistence, so a later reader cannot mistake a first pick for a standard.
licensingDecision.transport: Relayed by the commander in chat, inside gpt-architect's round-45 review text, and transcribed by claude-lead. Not machine-attested. Recorded as a human-commander decision rather than self-certified by the implementing agent, which is what control/policies.json requires: escalation.humanOnly lists Licensing, and selecting a catalog source is exactly that.
notCoveredByThisDecision: Any credentialed source. TMDB and anything else requiring an API key remains a separate Credentials escalation and is untouched by this.
Whether bulk ingestion engages the EU/UK sui generis database right. That question applies to Wikidata as much as to any other candidate and is for counsel, not for this record.
Commercial use terms for any future source. Only Wikidata's CC0 position on structured data was evidenced.
licensingDecision.obligationsThatFollow: Wikidata's structured data is CC0, but access is not unconditional: the Wikimedia User-Agent policy requires an informative User-Agent with contact information or the client may be IP-blocked without notice, and browser-impersonating agents are forbidden. That is why CatalogDocumentOptions.userAgent is required with no default, and it must stay that way. Text outside the main, property and lexeme namespaces is CC BY-SA rather than CC0, so the distinction has to survive into whatever is ingested.

review.title: Fixture provider states the protection fact it actually knows
review.acceptance: The fixture provider adapter emits contentProtection { state: "clear" } for its own candidates, because for a fixture the absence of DRM is a fact the adapter genuinely knows rather than something it is guessing. Created from gpt-architect's round-44 non-blocking finding on PL-0501, in the reviewer's own words: "Create a provider-owned task for the fixture provider protection fact. The fixture adapter, not PL-0501, should emit { state: \"clear\" } when that fact is genuinely known. PL-0501 may keep PROTECTION_NOT_STATED as the conservative fallback until that provider task lands." So the deliverable is a narrowing of where the fact is asserted, not a behaviour change in routing: PROTECTION_NOT_STATED stays in PL-0501 as the fallback for every adapter that has not stated a protection fact, and this task removes the fixture from the set that needs it. Required, and each is a way this task could be done wrongly: the fixture must set the field itself rather than PL-0501 special-casing the fixture provider id, because a consumer branching on a provider identity is exactly the provider-specific logic outside @liberty/provider-sdk that invariant 3 forbids; requiresContentDecryptionModule must be observed returning false for a fixture candidate and the observation recorded, since state !== "clear" is the whole point of the encoding and an untested clear is indistinguishable from an untested unknown; the fallback path in PL-0501 must be left in place and a test must still cover an adapter that states nothing, because deleting the fallback once its only current user stops needing it would fail open for the next adapter; and no other adapter may be given a protection fact here, because for a real provider the honest value is unknown and asserting clear for one would be a rights misstatement rather than a defaulting decision. Out of scope: any change to contract shape (PL-0902 owns it), to ranking (@liberty/media-engine), or to capability routing.

review.title: Playback session route refuses an oversized request body
review.acceptance: The production playback-session route refuses a request body above a declared bound before parsing it, and the refusal carries a reason code that exists in the contract. TODAY IT READS AN UNBOUNDED BODY: apps/web/src/app/api/v1/playback/session/playback-session-implementation.ts reads the body with no cap while the development-only resolve scaffold beside it caps one, so the production path is the weaker of the two. This is a task rather than a line in PL-0702 because the fix cannot be made honestly inside that task's surface: there is no reason code for an oversized body, adding one changes API behaviour, and invariant 5 requires docs/API_CONTRACTS.md to change first or deliberately alongside. Required: the bound is a named constant with the reason for its value, not a magic number; the reason code is added to the contract and to docs/API_CONTRACTS.md in the same change; the refusal happens BEFORE the body is buffered, because a cap enforced after reading the whole body does not bound memory; a regression drives a body over the bound through the real route and observes the refusal, and a second drives one just under it and observes normal handling, since a cap that refuses everything is indistinguishable from an outage. Out of scope: the candidate-id bound, which is PL-0708, and any change to what a well-formed request means.

THE HEADER IS NOT THE BOUND, which is the part worth reading: chunked encoding carries no content-length and the header is trivially forged, so content-length is consulted only to refuse EARLIER, and the actual control is a metered read of request.body that stops the instant the running total exceeds the cap and cancels the reader on every exit path -- peak memory is the bound plus one chunk whatever the header claimed. The gate consumes the stream and replays the bounded bytes as a new Request so the seam keeps its shape; a test asserts the replay is byte-for-byte. The outage guard -- a body just under the bound returning 200 granted -- PASSED at HEAD, correctly, because it is not a defect probe. Fixtures are sized from a local literal rather than from the constant under test, because a fixture sized from MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES degenerates to a tiny body on a tree where the constant does not exist, which would have made the red observation dishonest; a separate test ties the literal to the exported constant. Both build targets are covered by one cap in handler.ts, and the desktop test asserts 413 with remote.calls EMPTY, so an oversized body is never relayed to our own backend.

review.title: Stream candidate fields carry length bounds
review.acceptance: streamCandidateSchema bounds the length of its string fields, so a candidate cannot amplify a response. MEASURED, not hypothesised: a 1,000,000-character candidate id produced a 2,002,555-byte response during the PL-0702 review. The bound belongs in the contract rather than at the route, because every consumer of a candidate inherits it there and a per-route cap is one route away from being forgotten. Required: each bounded field's limit is justified against a real identifier rather than picked round -- state what the longest legitimate value looks like; a property test asserts no candidate accepted by the schema can exceed the response budget; and the change is checked against the fixture and Wikidata sources, because a bound that rejects a legitimate upstream id is an outage, not a fix. THE RISK THIS TASK CARRIES: streamCandidateSchema is the ranker's input and PL-0902 extends it; a bound set too low silently drops candidates and the reason trail must say so rather than showing an empty list. Out of scope: the request body bound (PL-0707).

review.title: Egress host classification folds the DNS root label
review.acceptance: packages/media-inspection/src/egress.ts classifies a fully qualified name the same as its dotless spelling, matching the fix PL-0702 made in packages/provider-sdk/src/stremio/url-policy.ts. THIS IS LOWER PRIORITY THAN IT SOUNDS AND THE REASON MUST NOT BE LOST: this path fails CLOSED -- an unrecognised spelling is refused rather than permitted -- so it is an inconsistency between two classifiers, not a bypass. It is filed anyway because two classifiers disagreeing about what a host is will eventually be reconciled by someone copying the wrong one. Required: the fix is the same narrowing (fold the root label before comparison, refuse an empty label rather than repairing it); a test asserts the two classifiers agree on a shared table of hostile spellings, so the next divergence fails a test rather than waiting for a review; and the fail-closed behaviour is preserved and asserted, because making this path agree with the other one must not make it permissive. Out of scope: merging the two classifiers into one, which is the resolve-and-pin question and belongs to PL-0710.

GREEN: 35 passed. A FINDING THE FIX PRODUCED, sharper than the one filed: before the change hostOnAllowlist('..', ['..']) returned TRUE, and so did hostOnAllowlist('cdn.example.test..', ['cdn.example.test..']) -- the old code treated a leading-dot entry as a suffix without validating it, so a string naming no host was matchable, and an entry repaired down to empty is the empty suffix, which matches every host there is. It never reached production behaviour because classifyHost refuses those with url_host_unparseable before the allowlist is consulted, so fail-closed held, but the function alone said yes. MUTATION-CHECKED: the tempting permissive fix, return host.replace(/\.+$/, '') -- fold until it stops instead of refusing -- makes 3 tests fail, so the fail-closed assertions are not vacuous. FAIL-CLOSED PRESERVED AND ASSERTED in both directions: empty allowlist still fetches nothing for every spelling in the table; the leading-dot rule still means strict subdomain; and the controls in front of and behind the allowlist still run, including url_host_private_literal for metadata.google.internal. EVEN WITH THAT HOST EXPLICITLY ALLOWLISTED. Folding admits exactly one thing that was refused before: another spelling of a name the operator already wrote down. The shared hostile-spelling table drives BOTH real implementations from one source, so the next divergence fails a test.

review.title: An agent instruction file has provenance, or it is not an instruction
review.acceptance: Repository validation detects any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md under a working directory that is not on an explicit, reviewed allowlist, and the authoritative instruction hierarchy is stated somewhere an agent reads before it starts. THE CONCRETE CASE: apps/web/AGENTS.md is GENERATED BY next dev and instructs agents to read node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing code. Nothing acted on it, and it is almost certainly benign. The finding is not that file -- it is that framework tooling can write an instruction file into a directory agents treat as authoritative, which makes a dependency's postinstall a path into the control plane's instruction surface. Required: the allowlist names each legitimate instruction file and who owns it, so an unowned one is a validation failure rather than a judgement call; generated instruction files are either gitignored and removed or allowlisted after being read, and the choice is recorded per file; validation fails on an unexpected file rather than warning, because a warning in a passing run is not a control; a regression plants an unexpected AGENTS.md and observes the failure, since a detector nobody has seen fire is not known to work; and the instruction hierarchy is written down -- which file wins, and that nothing under node_modules is ever authoritative. WHAT THIS TASK MUST NOT DO: silently delete a file a framework needs, or treat allowlisting as review. An allowlisted generated file must have been READ by a human or an agent that reports what it says.

recommended.title: Contract module boundaries
recommended.acceptance: Shared vocabularies live in their own leaf modules, domain contracts live in one module each, index.ts is a re-export-only compatibility barrel rather than the authoritative public surface, and a wildcard exports map lets a new domain contract be added without touching package metadata or the barrel; no cycle-driven z.lazy remains and structural regressions prove the boundary rather than merely reflecting it; no schema behaviour changes

recommended.title: Profile model
recommended.acceptance: Profiles are modelled above authentication rather than inside the auth library, with the active profile carried alongside the session rather than inside the identity record; profile scoping is present in the first migration rather than retrofitted, because that is the part that is expensive to reverse; profiles can be created and selected with authorization tests

recommended.title: Provider outbound HTTP resolves, classifies and pins its destination
recommended.acceptance: Provider outbound HTTP adopts the existing @liberty/media-inspection resolve-and-pin control (authoriseFetchTarget / nodePinnedFetch) instead of classifying host literals. Required, and each clause is a separate way host-literal checking fails: DNS resolution happens BEFORE the outbound connection; EVERY resolved address is classified, not just the first; the request is refused if ANY resolved address is private, loopback, link-local or reserved, unless an explicitly permitted local-only path applies; the connection is PINNED to the approved resolved address, so DNS rebinding cannot change the destination between the check and the connect; redirects repeat resolution, classification and pinning PER HOP; and TLS hostname verification and SNI are not regressed -- pinning to an address must still present and verify the name. Tests are required for public-name-to-private-IP, DNS rebinding, mixed public/private answer sets, and translation-prefix cases. WHY THIS IS P0 AND WHY IT IS FILED NOW: F1, F7 and F8 are three defects of ONE SHAPE in one function -- a host spelling the string comparisons did not anticipate, each reading as public, none findable by reading. A check that compares a string against literals is only ever as complete as the list of spellings whoever wrote it thought of. Resolve-and-pin classifies the address a resolver returned, which has one spelling.
recommended.notes: Created 2026-09-18 on gpt-architect's round-46 instruction, reviewing PL-0702 at bbfaa5a997e6ee146271f26e5b2546b7e67e47d2. recommended.title: Provider health contract
recommended.acceptance: A provider with zero observations reports unknown with a null observed success rate and a zero sample count, never a mid-range score and never a pass; any prior used to rank an unobserved provider is labelled as a prior rather than presented as measured availability; degraded-but-usable is a state distinct from up and down; health output is pure over the observations plus an explicit policy version, with no hidden wall-clock decay; and health never affects entitlement, so a provider at perfect health still cannot make an unauthorized candidate eligible

typecheck.evidence: turbo run typecheck --filter @liberty/provider-sdk exit 0 under pinned Node 22 resolved via npx node@22.

unit.evidence: turbo run test --filter @liberty/provider-sdk exit 0 under pinned Node 22: zero observations yielding unknown with a null observed rate and a zero sample count, a prior labelled rather than presented as measurement at the same ranking number as a measured value, the degraded band held distinct from up and down, purity over observations plus an explicit policy version with Date.now replaced by a thrower to prove no wall clock is read, whole-report permutation invariance under generated policies, monotonicity in each count, and a compile-time guard that no health type can carry entitlement.
